name: Enon
label: Touch and Go
lede: After Brainiac ended, John Schmersal built a band around a junk-kit drummer and a Moog, lost his label to 9/11, and found a co-singer in a bassist who had just quit her last band.

eras.title: Out of Brainiac's wreckage
eras.text: Brainiac ended the day Tim Taylor died. John Schmersal moved to New York, made a solo record, then started a band that kept Brainiac's synths and humor and let the melodies through.

years.h: Tim Taylor dies, and Brainiac ends with him
years.p: [[Brainiac|8db9ae5b-4412-434a-aedd-dc2bb316c355]] singer [[Tim Taylor|01a4d435-701d-47e4-b250-42bcd7bef7b8]] dies in a car crash near Dayton, and the band is over. Guitarist [[John Schmersal|9f0f837b-e427-4611-aef4-5db88298bfaf]] records a 4-track album as John Stuart Mill, Forget Everything, in an abandoned Masonic temple in Kentucky.
years.xp: The solo record came out in 1999 on See Thru Broadcasting, went out of print when that label folded, and was reissued on vinyl by Columbus's Scioto Records in 2016.

years.h: Two players from Skeleton Key join Schmersal, and Enon begins
years.p: Rick Lee and Steve Calhoon of Skeleton Key, a band Brainiac had toured with, sign on. The name comes from Enon, Ohio, a village near Schmersal's hometown of Dayton.
years.xp:
Schmersal told the Quietus he wanted something that extended where Brainiac had been going, "synthesizers, guitar tunings, futuristic ideas and humour," but "not be afraid to be more purely melodic." He chased Lee in particular for his sampler work.

Lee played a junk kit: a Radio Flyer wagon, a propane tank and old hubcaps.

years.h: Believo!, produced by David Sardy for his own label
years.p: David Sardy produces the debut and releases it on See Thru Broadcasting. The Washington Post praised "Get the Letter Out" for daring to be tuneful.

years.cap: John Schmersal on stage with Enon
years.h: Toko Yasuda, just out of the Lapse, takes a copy of Believo! and joins
years.p: The trio wanted more low end. Schmersal met [[Toko Yasuda|b4aeb2ed-0b11-4f24-9479-77de69334918]], a former bassist in [[Blonde Redhead|6821bf3f-5d5b-4b0f-8fa4-79d2ab2d9219]] and the Van Pelt, right after she quit the Lapse; [[Matt Schulz|4e40bd31-1ce7-4b96-8757-c7872ad8d76a]] later took over the drums from Calhoon, who couldn't commit to touring.
years.xp: Yasuda, who grew up in Fujisawa and Kamakura and moved to New York in 1992, went on to sing lead on much of the next album.

eras.title: Touch and Go catches a stranded record
eras.text: The second album was finished and scheduled when its label shut down. Touch and Go picked it up, and the band started giving music away online every month.

years.cap: Schmersal at the Bowery Ballroom, New York
years.h: See Thru Broadcasting folds after 9/11, with Enon's album due
years.p: High Society was set for September 25, 2001. After the attacks in New York the label closed, and the band put out the instrumental On Hold to tide fans over.

years.h: A free song every month, gone when the month ends
years.p: From April 2002 to December 2003, Enon post an unreleased song a month on their site as a 128 kbit/s MP3, available only for that month.

years.h: High Society lands on Touch and Go after half a year in limbo
years.p: Yasuda sings lead on most of it. Pitchfork's Rob Mitchum gave it an 8.8 and called it Schmersal's first firm steps away from Brainiac; the band toured with the Faint.

years.h: Backstage at the Met in Providence with a George Foreman grill
years.p: Schmersal and Yasuda cook for the web series Cooking with Rockstars, in a noisy backstage area at the Providence club.

yt: "Daughter in the House of Fools" (Touch and Go)
years.h: Hocus Pocus hides a web address under the CD tray
years.p: Lift the black disc holder and there's a URL to a hidden site. Rick Lee had left after High Society; reviews were mixed, with praise for Schmersal and Yasuda trading vocals on "Murder Sounds" and "Starcastic."

eras.title: A house in Philadelphia
eras.text: Schmersal bought a house in Philadelphia, Yasuda followed after being priced out of New York, and his scoring work for cartoons and TV kept growing. One more album came out of the Philadelphia years.

years.h: Lost Marbles and Exploded Evidence: the singles, plus a DVD
years.p: Singles and hard-to-find web songs, with a separate DVD of live footage and videos. Azealia Banks's "Gimme a Chance" later sampled "Knock That Door" from it.

years.cap: Enon at the Dumbo Arts Festival, Brooklyn, October 2005
years.src: Lazy-i · Wikipedia: Toko Yasuda · Wikipedia: Enon
years.h: Schmersal buys a house in Philadelphia and builds a studio
years.p: The longtime New Yorker told Lazy-i he planned a basement practice space. Yasuda moved too after being priced out of Manhattan and Brooklyn, and the New York Times cited the band in a piece on Philadelphia as the "sixth borough."
years.xp: Bands including Mean Reds and Thunderbirds Are Now! recorded with Schmersal there. His day work grew to Disney, Cartoon Network, MTV, Nickelodeon and Sundance Channel, plus scoring on Monster House with Sardy.

years.cap: Enon at the Echo, Los Angeles, November 2007
years.h: All three Enon members play on Les Savy Fav's Let's Stay Friends
years.p: Schulz drums on two songs; Yasuda had already sung on Les Savy Fav's The Cat and the Cobra.

years.h: Grass Geysers...Carbon Clouds leaks a month early
years.p: The last Enon album hit the internet on September 5. Reviews ran warmer than for Hocus Pocus, and Touch and Go reissued Believo! the same day, videos included.

years.cap: Schmersal with Enon at Primavera Sound, Barcelona, May 2008
years.h: Matt Schulz leaves and ends up drumming for Holy Fuck
years.p: Schulz announces he is leaving to pursue other interests and joins [[Holy Fuck|4342cf80-7c06-4402-a431-457e77310474]] as a touring member.

yt: "We Are the Robots" on Yo Gabba Gabba!
years.h: Robots doing chores to an Enon song on Yo Gabba Gabba!
years.p: The otherwise unreleased "We Are the Robots," 1 minute 21 seconds long, plays over animated robots helping kids with housework. In 2009 Schmersal and Yasuda wrote the theme for PBS Kids' Dash's Dance Party.

eras.title: On the road with Caribou
eras.text: Schmersal toured as Caribou's guitarist through much of 2010 and 2011, and in a 2011 interview called Enon finished.

years.h: Asked about a follow-up, Schmersal says no
years.p: John Schmersal tells the blog Fucking Nostalgic, in the middle of touring with Caribou: 180-some shows in eight months.
years.xp: Three years later he gave the Quietus the whole explanation: "We just got to a point where none of us was interested in proceeding with it anymore."

eras.title: Everyone lands somewhere
eras.text: Yasuda became a touring fixture for other people's bands, Schmersal kept starting new ones, and Brainiac came back.

years.h: Yasuda joins St. Vincent on the road
years.p: She plays synth, bass and guitar on [[St. Vincent|5334edc0-5faf-4ca5-b1df-000de3e1f752]]'s Strange Mercy tour and later ones, and sings on "Masseduction." She later toured with [[Sleater-Kinney|e36e78eb-3ace-4acd-882c-16789e700ab7]] and Cate Le Bon.

years.h: Plvs Vltra: Yasuda's solo album, produced by Schmersal
years.p: Parthenon comes out on Spectrum Spools, with Danny Ray Thompson of the Sun Ra Arkestra among the guests.

years.h: Vertical Scratchers, with Robert Pollard dropping in
years.p: Schmersal's duo with drummer Christian Eric Beaulieu releases Daughter of Everything on Merge, with fellow Daytonian Robert Pollard of [[Guided by Voices|6c85f4c3-026c-4c16-9a7c-f546f42ed0fb]] as a guest. Pitchfork gave it a 7.2.

years.cap: Brainiac on their reunion run, June 2023
years.h: Touch and Go reissues Believo! again, as Brainiac returns
years.p: The debut gets its second Touch and Go reissue while Schmersal fronts the revived Brainiac, singing the songs of the band Enon grew out of.

sources.title: The Quietus: Life After Brainiac, John Schmersal interviewed (2014)
